description: Pi host firewall is now applied automatically: the captive-portal-web container re-derives the user-VLAN allow-list (scripts/pi-host-firewall.sh) from .env at every start-up, exactly like the DNS-hijack iptables rules. The separate systemd unit (bf-host-firewall.service) is removed. Also: ip6tables added to the web container's sudo rules so the IPv6 part of the firewall can be applied.

add.description: Already in .env from the previous update, but it now has an effect: true = the web container applies the host firewall on every start-up (user VLANs may reach the Pi only for DHCP, DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, the pre-auth relay port, NTP, ICMP); false = the web container REMOVES the firewall on start-up. Loopback (VPS tunnels / VS Code SSH), established connections, the management VLAN and the Wi-Fi/ISP side are never restricted. Leave true unless you need to disable it.

Confirm before the firewall becomes automatic: 1 = also allow SSH (tcp/22) to the Pi from user VLANs; 0 = SSH only from the management VLAN, Wi-Fi/ISP LAN or the Oracle VPS tunnel. Set 1 only if you administer the Pi from a device on a user VLAN.

notes: No database changes. After updating: (1) `docker compose build web` is recommended (the Dockerfile sudoers list gained ip6tables); without it the firewall still applies for IPv4 and logs 'ip6tables unavailable or not permitted; skipping IPv6 rules'. (2) Restart web. About 10 s later `docker compose logs web | grep -i 'host firewall'` should show 'Host firewall apply ok' with one line per user VLAN; `sudo scripts/pi-host-firewall.sh status` shows the chains and drop counters. (3) If a previous installer run created bf-host-firewall.service on this host, retire it (the web container now owns the rules): `sudo systemctl disable --now bf-host-firewall.service; sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/bf-host-firewall.service; sudo systemctl daemon-reload`. Leaving it in place is harmless (both apply the same idempotent rules). (4) Rollback to 0286010 keeps whatever rules are currently loaded until the next reboot; `sudo scripts/pi-host-firewall.sh remove` clears them immediately.
